_purpose: Target Cache-Control policy for richenquest.com. Applied at the Catalyst hosting layer alongside infra/security-headers.json during the M4 spike. Exists so the deployment-verification pass has an EXPECTED value to diff against, rather than accepting whatever the host defaults to.
_why_it_matters: site.css and main.js are requested with ?v=<hash>, a content hash the build derives and stamps. Cache-busting query strings only buy anything if something sets a long TTL against them — otherwise every repeat visitor re-downloads assets that never changed. Lighthouse measures a cold first visit; real users on Indian and Nepali mobile networks are returning visitors, and their experience is governed entirely by these headers.

rules._why: Content-hashed via ?v=. Safe to cache for a year: a change produces a new URL.
One week, NOT immutable. These are NOT covered by the build hash (see caveat below), so a long TTL would strand a stale icon sprite in browser caches.
HTML is the entry point that references the hashed assets. It must revalidate so a deploy is visible immediately; the 304 is cheap.
Crawler-facing. An hour keeps them fresh for Search Console without hammering origin.

_known_caveat: build.mjs:149 derives the cache-bust hash from CSS + JS only — createHash().update(css + jsConcat). Images and assets/img/icons.svg (referenced 29x on the homepage via <use href>) are NOT in the hash and carry no version query. That is why the image rule above is one week rather than immutable. Folding all of assets/ into the hash input would let images move to immutable too; tracked as a Medium finding in the 2026-08-12 audit.
_verify_on_deploy: curl -sI <url>/assets/css/site.css | grep -i cache-control  — and confirm the ?v= hash in the served HTML matches a local rebuild of the deployed commit (the build is deterministic).
